polis#definition: The Greek city-state, consisting of a city with its surrounding land and the community of its citizens, who governed themselves. There were hundreds of poleis, from Athens and Sparta to small island towns; their independence and rivalry shaped Greek history. The word politics derives from polis.
prinzipat#definition: The form of rule established by Augustus in 27 BC, in which the emperor appeared as princeps, the first among equals, and formally left the republican institutions such as the Senate and the consuls in place. In fact power over the army, the provinces and the finances lay with the emperor. The Principate lasted until the crisis of the 3rd century.
reconquista#definition: The reconquest of the Iberian Peninsula by the Christian kingdoms of Asturias, León, Castile, Aragón and Portugal, which lasted from the 8th century to the fall of Granada in 1492. It did not proceed as an uninterrupted war, but with long phases of alliances, trade and cultural exchange across the frontier. After 1492 Jews and Muslims were expelled or forced to be baptized, which put an end to the religious diversity of Spain.
reformation#definition: A movement of religious renewal which began in 1517 with Luther's 95 Theses and led to the division of Western Christendom into Catholics and Protestants. Its adherents appealed to scripture and faith alone, rejected indulgences and papal authority, and created churches of their own in Germany, Switzerland, Scandinavia, England and the Netherlands.
reparationen#definition: Payments and deliveries in kind which the loser of a war must render to the victors as compensation for war damage. The Treaty of Versailles imposed reparations on Germany which were fixed in 1921 at 132 billion gold marks and included coal, locomotives and ships. The dispute over the payments led to the occupation of the Ruhr and was temporarily eased by the Dawes Plan of 1924 and the Young Plan of 1929, until the payments effectively ended in 1932.
restauration#definition: The policy after 1815 which, proceeding from the Congress of Vienna, sought to restore the rule of the old dynasties and to push back the ideas of the Revolution. Its means were censorship, police surveillance, the banning of political associations and interventions against uprisings in Spain, Italy and Germany. Its most important representative was the Austrian state chancellor Metternich.
romanisierung#definition: The adoption of the Roman language, way of life, legal order and style of town building by the population of the conquered provinces. It happened not through compulsion but through the settlement of veterans, trade, citizenship for the local elites and the attraction of baths, theaters and roads. Out of the Latin of the provinces the Romance languages emerged.
sakoku#definition: The Japanese term for the closing of the country under the Tokugawa shogunate from 1639 to 1854. Foreigners were not allowed to enter, Japanese were not allowed to leave the country, and foreign trade remained restricted to Chinese and Dutch merchants at Nagasaki; the country experienced two centuries of peace with only very limited European influence (Western learning still arrived via the Dutch as rangaku).
satrapie#definition: A province of the Persian Empire, administered by a governor, the satrap, in the name of the Great King. The satraps collected taxes, provided troops and administered justice, but were supervised by royal inspectors. The system allowed the Achaemenids to hold together an empire of many peoples and languages.
scholastik#definition: The scholarly method of the medieval universities, which examined questions of faith with the means of logic and the philosophy of Aristotle. Theses were tested in regulated disputations and objections refuted; Thomas Aquinas brought scholasticism to its high point in the 13th century.
seidenstrasse#definition: A network of caravan routes and sea routes which from the Han period onward connected China by way of Central Asia and Persia with India and the Mediterranean world. Alongside silk, spices, glass and horses, religions such as Buddhism, techniques such as papermaking, and diseases also traveled along it. The name dates only from the 19th century.
senat#definition: The council of Rome's former officeholders, originally of the elders, with about 300 to 600 members appointed for life. In the Republic the Senate determined foreign policy, finances and provincial administration and was the center of the nobility's power. In the imperial period it lost influence, but survived as an honorary assembly into late antiquity.
soziale-frage#definition: The term for the distress of the working class in the 19th century: low wages, long working hours, child labor, wretched housing and the absence of provision for sickness and old age. Churches, entrepreneurs, socialists and the state sought different answers, from company housing through trade unions to social insurance.
sozialversicherung#definition: Compulsory insurance organized by the state which protects employees against sickness, accident, old age and disability and is financed by contributions from employers and employees. It was introduced by Bismarck in the German Empire between 1883 and 1889 and became a model for welfare states all over the world.
stadtstaat#definition: An independent state consisting of a city and its surrounding land. In Sumer each city-state was dedicated to a god of its own and was ruled by a king or priestly prince; the cities fought one another over water and land until Sargon of Akkad united them into a single empire.
staendegesellschaft#definition: The division of medieval society into estates by birth, with different rights and duties: the clergy, the nobility and the great remainder of peasants and townspeople. According to the doctrine of the time, the first prayed, the second fought and the third worked; uprisings such as that of 1381 in England called this order into question.
stellungskrieg#definition: A way of waging war in which opposing armies face each other in fortified trenches and the front scarcely moves for months or years. On the Western Front of the First World War, machine guns, artillery and barbed wire made every attack so costly that both sides remained in their trenches until 1918. Verdun and the Somme are the best-known examples.
stellvertreterkrieg#definition: A war in which great powers do not fight each other themselves but support hostile parties in a third country with weapons, money, advisers or troops of their own. In the Cold War the USA and the Soviet Union carried out their opposition in this way in Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan and Africa. Those who suffered were above all the populations of these countries.
sufismus#definition: The mystical current of Islam, which strives for an immediate, loving experience of God and uses prayer, meditation, song, dance and asceticism to that end. Sufis such as Rabia of Basra, al-Ghazali and Rumi created important poetry and philosophy; from the 12th century onward they joined together in orders with masters and disciples. Sufi brotherhoods carried Islam to Anatolia, India, Southeast Asia and Africa.
sunniten-und-schiiten#definition: The two great currents of Islam, which arose out of the dispute over the succession to Muhammad. The Shiites regard Ali, the Prophet's cousin and son-in-law, and his descendants as the only legitimate leaders; the Sunnis recognize the elected caliphs and appeal to the Sunna, the example of the Prophet. Around 85 to 90 percent of Muslims today are Sunnis; Shiites live above all in Iran, Iraq, Lebanon and Bahrain.
totaler-krieg#definition: A war in which a state mobilizes all its people, economic forces and resources for the struggle and the line between soldiers and civilians becomes blurred. The First World War is regarded as the first total war: factories produced only for the front, women replaced men at work, and blockades left the civilian population to go hungry. Propaganda and censorship were meant to secure the will to hold out.
tragoedie#definition: A serious drama which arose in Athens in the 5th century BC out of the choral songs in honor of Dionysus. The tragedies of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides show heroes from myth and history in conflict with the gods, the law and fate, and were performed at competitions before thousands of citizens.
tyrannis#definition: The sole rule of a man who seized power without any legal basis, usually by force or with the support of the people against the nobility. In the 7th and 6th centuries BC tyrants ruled in many Greek cities and often promoted the economy and the arts; only later did the term become an expression for violent despotism.
vernichtungskrieg#definition: The term for the German war against the Soviet Union from 1941, which from the outset aimed not merely at military victory but at the destruction of the state, the murder of the Jews and of communist officials, and the death by starvation of millions of civilians and prisoners of war. Orders such as the Commissar Order suspended the law of war. The Wehrmacht was directly involved in this.
voelkerbundsmandat#definition: A territory which after the First World War was detached from the possessions of Germany or of the Ottoman Empire and administered by a victorious power on behalf of the League of Nations, supposedly until it was ready for independence. Great Britain received Palestine, Iraq and Transjordan, France Syria and Lebanon; the German colonies went to Great Britain, France, Belgium, Japan and others. In practice the mandates differed hardly at all from colonies.
voelkerwanderung#definition: The period from the invasion of the Huns around 375 to about 568, in which Germanic peoples such as the Goths, Vandals, Franks and Lombards pushed into the Roman Empire and founded kingdoms of their own there. It led to the fall of the Western Roman Empire in 476 and to the emergence of the medieval states of Europe; its causes were the search for land, population pressure and the pressure of the Huns.
volkssouveraenitaet#definition: The principle that all state power proceeds from the people and that rulers exercise their power only as agents of the people. It was formulated by Rousseau, anchored in 1776 in the American Declaration of Independence and in 1789 in the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, and replaced the divine right of kings. Popular sovereignty is to this day the foundation of democratic constitutions.
vormaerz#definition: The period in Germany between the Congress of Vienna in 1815 and the March Revolution of 1848, in which liberal and national movements grew despite censorship and persecution. Student fraternities, the Hambach Festival, writers such as Heine and Büchner, and uprisings such as that of the Silesian weavers marked these years. The term looks back from the Revolution of 1848 to the time before it.
weimarer-republik#definition: The name for the German state from 1918 to 1933, after the city of Weimar, where the National Assembly adopted the constitution in 1919. The first German democracy stood from the beginning under the pressure of the Treaty of Versailles, inflation, attempted coups and political violence. After a brief stabilization in the Golden Twenties it broke apart under the Great Depression and ended with Hitler's appointment as Reich Chancellor.
wettlauf-um-afrika#definition: The rapid division of almost the entire African continent among the European colonial powers between about 1880 and 1914. The Berlin Conference of 1884/85 laid down the rules of the game, without any Africans taking part. Borders were drawn on the drawing board and in many cases still exist today.
widerstand#definition: A collective term for all forms of opposition to the Nazi regime, from the refusal to give the Hitler salute through leaflets and the hiding of the persecuted to assassination attempts and plans for a coup. It was carried by communists and social democrats, Christians, students, officers and individuals acting alone such as Georg Elser, but it always remained a small minority. In the occupied countries partisans and underground movements such as the Résistance fought against German rule.
zikkurat#definition: A stepped temple tower of mud brick in Mesopotamia, on whose summit stood a sanctuary of the city god. The ziggurat of Ur, from around 2100 BC, is the best preserved; the biblical Tower of Babel goes back to the ziggurat of Babylon.
transsaharahandel#definition: Long-distance trade by camel caravans across the Sahara between North Africa and West Africa. From the south came mainly gold, ivory and slaves, from the north salt, horses, cloth and books; Islam also spread with the traders. The trade formed the basis of the empires of Ghana, Mali and Songhai.
griot#definition: In West Africa, a hereditary singer, storyteller and musician who passes on genealogies, praise songs and the history of ruling families orally. Griots served as advisers at the courts and still preserve epics such as that of Sundiata today.
mansa#definition: Title of the ruler of the Mali Empire in the Malinke language, roughly translatable as king or emperor. The mansa stood at the head of a federation of provinces and tributary princes; the most famous holder of the title was Mansa Musa.
swahili#definition: Bantu language and culture of the trading cities on the East African coast between Somalia and Mozambique. It arose from African roots in exchange with Arab, Persian and Indian merchants, is mostly shaped by Islam and adopted many Arabic loanwords. Swahili is today one of the most widely spoken languages in Africa.
oba#definition: Title of the kings in the kingdom of Benin and in several Yoruba states. The oba of Benin was regarded as a sacred ruler who had authority over land and people and whose ancestors were honored with commemorative heads and relief plaques of brass.
geez#definition: Ancient Semitic language and script of Ethiopia, attested since the time of Aksum. Ge'ez disappeared as a spoken language in the Middle Ages but has remained the language of the Ethiopian Orthodox liturgy to this day; the alphabets of Amharic and Tigrinya developed from its script.
goldener-stuhl#definition: Sacred symbol of the Asante Empire which, according to tradition, descended from the sky under Osei Tutu and embodies the soul of the people. No one may sit on it; the asantehene is installed over it.
mfecane#definition: Term for the wars, flights and state foundations in southern Africa between roughly 1815 and 1840; in Nguni languages the word means something like crushing. Its causes and extent are disputed among historians.
mesoamerika#definition: A cultural area comprising southern and central Mexico, Guatemala, Belize and parts of Honduras and El Salvador. Despite their different languages, its peoples shared maize farming, pyramid temples, the ball game, a 260-day ritual calendar and many gods. They included the Olmecs, Zapotecs, Maya, Teotihuacan, Toltecs and Aztecs.
lange-zaehlung#definition: A Mesoamerican system of reckoning time that counts the days since a mythical starting date in 3114 BC. It uses units of 1, 20, 360, 7,200 and 144,000 days and allowed dating to the exact day over centuries. The Maya used it on stelae from about the 3rd to the early 10th century.
mesoamerikanisches-ballspiel#definition: A team game with a heavy rubber ball that usually could only be played with the hips, buttocks and thighs. It was played for over 3,000 years throughout Mesoamerica on long courts bounded by walls. The game was sport, religious ritual and sometimes part of political ceremonies that could end with sacrifices.
chinampa#definition: An artificially built-up, rectangular garden plot in shallow lakes and swamps, bordered by canals. Mud and plant remains kept the soil fertile, so that several harvests a year were possible. The chinampas in the Valley of Mexico fed the great city of Tenochtitlan and are still farmed in Xochimilco today.
quipu#definition: A knotted cord of cotton or wool with which information was recorded in the Andes. Many pendant cords hung from a main cord, and their knots indicated numbers such as inhabitants, levies and stores in the decimal system. Specialists, the quipucamayocs, read and made the quipus; whether they also recorded language is still unresolved.
ayllu#definition: A kin and village community in the Andes whose members traced themselves to a common ancestor. The ayllu held land in common, distributed it to families and organized mutual help in fieldwork and house building. In the Inca empire it formed the basic unit for levies and labor service; it survives in many Andean villages to this day.
tlatoani#definition: The title of the rulers in the city-states of central Mexico; the Nahuatl word means "the one who speaks". The tlatoani of Tenochtitlan was chosen by a council from among the men of the ruling family and was supreme commander, judge and mediator with the gods. As huey tlatoani, great speaker, he stood at the head of the Triple Alliance.
erdhuegelkulturen#definition: A collective term for Indigenous cultures of North America that built earthen mounds and embankments for graves, temples and ceremonies over thousands of years. They include Poverty Point, the Adena and Hopewell cultures and the Mississippian culture with Cahokia. In the 19th century white Americans often wrongly attributed the structures to a vanished foreign people instead of crediting them to the ancestors of the Indigenous peoples.
pax-mongolica#definition: Name for the period in the 13th and 14th centuries when the Mongol Empire ruled large parts of Eurasia and travellers and merchants could move relatively safely from China to Eastern Europe. Relay stations, unified rule and letters of safe conduct promoted the exchange of goods, knowledge and religions, but also the spread of the plague.
goldene-horde#definition: Mongol successor state in the steppes north of the Black and Caspian Seas, founded by Batu after the Mongol invasion around 1242, with its capital at Sarai on the Volga. The Russian princes had to pay it tribute and have their rule confirmed by the khan; this dependence ended in 1480.
shogunat#definition: Military government in Japan headed by a shogun, a supreme commander appointed by the emperor. From 1192 to 1868 the Kamakura, Ashikaga and Tokugawa shogunates ruled in succession, while the emperor in Kyoto performed mainly religious and ceremonial duties.
samurai#definition: Members of the Japanese warrior class, who originally served lords as armed retainers. In the Edo period they formed the highest of the four estates, were the only ones allowed to carry swords and in peacetime often worked as officials; their privileges were abolished in 1876.
hangeul#definition: The Korean alphabet that King Sejong had developed in 1443 and promulgated in 1446. Its letters stand for individual sounds and are combined into syllable blocks, which makes it much easier to learn than Chinese script.
tributsystem#definition: The framework of relations between China and its neighbours, in which foreign rulers sent envoys with gifts to the imperial court and thereby formally recognized the emperor as their overlord. In return they received valuable gifts, trading rights and protection; countries such as Korea, Vietnam and Malacca remained largely independent.
acht-banner#definition: The military and social organization of the Manchus, in which all families were assigned to eight units named after the colours of their flags. The banner troops conquered China in 1644 and thereafter, as privileged garrisons in the major cities, formed the backbone of Qing rule.
mansab-system#definition: The ranking system for office-holders in the Mughal Empire introduced by Akbar. Each mansabdar received a rank that determined his salary and the number of horsemen he had to provide for the ruler; the ranks were not hereditary and bound both Muslims and Hindu Rajputs to the court.
europaeische-union#definition: A union of European states that emerged from the European Communities in 1993 with the Treaty of Maastricht. Its members share a single market, common institutions such as the Parliament, the Commission and the Court of Justice, and for the most part the euro. After several enlargements and the departure of Great Britain, the EU comprises 27 states.
digitalisierung#definition: The conversion of information into digital data and the growing use of computers, the internet and networked devices in all areas of life. Since the 1990s it has fundamentally changed work, trade, communication, education and politics. Its downsides include surveillance, misuse of data and dependence on a few large companies.
soziale-medien#definition: Internet platforms on which users themselves publish, share and comment on texts, images and videos. They connect billions of people and enable rapid mobilization, for example in the Arab Spring or the MeToo movement. At the same time hate speech and disinformation spread through them, and their algorithms are held partly responsible for the polarization of societies.
kuenstliche-intelligenz#definition: Computer systems that solve tasks which previously required human thinking, such as understanding language, recognizing images or preparing decisions. Modern methods learn from large amounts of data instead of following firmly programmed rules. Since 2022 generative programs such as ChatGPT have become widespread and have sparked debates about work, copyright and control.
klimawandel#definition: The warming of the Earth caused by humans, above all through the burning of coal, oil and gas, which releases carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases. The consequences are rising sea levels and more heat waves, droughts and heavy rainfall. With the Paris Agreement of 2015 states aim to keep warming well below two degrees.
islamismus#definition: Political movements that seek to order state and society according to their interpretation of Islam and sharia. They range from parties that take part in elections to terrorist groups such as al-Qaeda or the so-called Islamic State. The term refers to a political ideology and not to the religion of Islam, the great majority of whose followers reject violence.
populismus#definition: A political style that sets a supposedly unified, true people against a corrupt elite and claims to represent the will of the people alone. There are populists on the right and the left; today they often turn against immigration, globalization and international institutions. Critics see in it a danger to minority rights, the separation of powers and independent media.
pandemie#definition: An infectious disease that spreads across countries and continents and affects a very large number of people. Well-known examples are the Black Death in the 14th century, the Spanish flu of 1918 to 1920 and the COVID-19 pandemic from 2020. Worldwide travel can accelerate the spread, while vaccines and hygiene contain it.
encomienda#definition: A Spanish colonial institution in which the Crown “entrusted” a group of Indigenous people to a Spaniard, to whom they owed tribute and labour. In return the encomendero was to protect them and have them instructed in the Christian faith. In practice the encomienda led to severe exploitation and was gradually pushed back after the New Laws of 1542.
mita#definition: Originally a labour service in the Inca Empire, which the Spaniards turned into a system of forced labour. Indigenous villages had to supply a share of their men in rotation for mines such as Potosí or for other work. The mita was one of the most hated burdens of the colonial era and was abolished only in the course of independence.
vizekoenigreich#definition: The largest administrative unit of the Spanish colonial empire, headed by a viceroy as the personal representative of the king. New Spain (1535) and Peru (1542) came first, and New Granada and Río de la Plata were added in the 18th century. Portugal later also appointed viceroys for Brazil.
kreolen#definition: In Spanish America, the term for descendants of Europeans born in the colonies. They often owned land, mines and trading houses, but were passed over for high offices in favour of those born in Spain. Creoles such as Simón Bolívar and José de San Martín led the independence movements.
mestizen#definition: The term for people with European and Indigenous ancestors in colonial Latin America. The colonial authorities classified the population by such categories of origin, which determined rights, taxes and status. In the 19th and 20th centuries mixing was declared part of the national identity in countries such as Mexico.
quilombo#definition: In Brazil, the term for a settlement of escaped enslaved people, often in forests or mountains that were difficult to reach. Quilombos ranged from small camps to large communities such as Palmares with their own agriculture and defence. Similar communities in Spanish America were called palenques.
jesuitenreduktion#definition: A mission village run by Jesuits, in which Indigenous people, above all Guaraní, were settled, Christianised and protected from slave raiders and colonists. The reductions had churches, workshops and common fields and were partly self-governing. After the expulsion of the Jesuits in 1767 they declined.
caudillo#definition: The term for a political and military leader who relied on a personal following, often armed horsemen and dependent rural workers. After independence caudillos shaped politics in many Latin American countries and frequently disregarded constitutions. To this day the term stands for authoritarian rule tailored to one person.
janitscharen#definition: The elite infantry of the Ottoman sultans, whose name means "new troops". They emerged in the 14th century, were recruited through the levy of boys, paid regularly and equipped early with firearms, which made them the first standing infantry in Europe. Later the Janissaries became a powerful group hostile to reform, until Mahmud II dissolved them in 1826.
devsirme#definition: The periodic levy of Christian boys, mainly from Balkan villages, for the sultan's service. The boys were converted to Islam and trained as Janissaries or in the palace; some rose to grand vizier, and the architect Sinan entered state service this way. In the 17th century the levy lost importance and was abandoned.
millet#definition: The term for the recognized religious communities of the Ottoman Empire, such as the Greek Orthodox Christians, the Armenians and the Jews. Under their religious heads they largely regulated marriage, inheritance, education and welfare themselves and were responsible to the sultan for taxes and order. The millet order was shaped into a fixed system above all in the 19th century.
grosswesir#definition: The highest minister of the Ottoman Empire and the sultan's deputy, who held his seal. He presided over the imperial council and the administration and often also commanded the army in the field. His official seat, the Sublime Porte, became the European name for the Ottoman government as a whole.
timar#definition: A grant under which a cavalryman, the sipahi, received the tax revenues of certain villages and in return had to go to war with equipment and retinue. The land remained the property of the state and was not hereditary. From the late 16th century the timar system lost importance and was increasingly replaced by tax farming.
harem#definition: The protected, private area of a Muslim household, especially the living quarters of the sultan's family in the Topkapı Palace. There lived the sultan's mother, his wives and concubines, children and female servants, and women were also educated there. Contrary to European fantasies, the harem was a political centre of power in which the valide sultan exercised great influence.
kapitulationen#definition: Trade privileges that the sultans granted to European states, for example France in 1569 and England in 1580. They allowed foreign merchants low customs duties, free exercise of religion and the jurisdiction of their own consuls. In the 19th century they became an instrument of European influence; the Ottoman Empire abrogated them unilaterally in 1914.
jungtuerken#definition: A movement of officers, officials and intellectuals that from the 1890s fought against the absolute rule of Abdülhamid II and for the constitution. Its most important organization, the Committee of Union and Progress, forced the restoration of the constitution in 1908 and dominated the state from 1913. Its government led the empire into the First World War and was responsible for the Armenian Genocide.
